subject: chemistry
title: Phenols and directing effects
key_idea: Phenol has an –OH group joined to a benzene ring. It is a weak acid, and the oxygen donates electrons into the ring, so phenol substitutes much more easily than benzene. Substituents on a ring direct new groups to the 2- and 4-positions, or to the 3-position.

blocks.text: In phenol, C₆H₅OH, the –OH group is attached directly to the ring. This section covers why it is a weak acid.

items: Phenol is a weak acid: C₆H₅OH ⇌ C₆H₅O⁻ + H⁺.
It reacts with sodium hydroxide, a neutralisation, to form sodium phenoxide and water.
It does **not** react with carbonates, so no carbon dioxide is given off.
Carboxylic acids do react with carbonates, so this separates them from phenols.
A lone pair on the oxygen of the phenoxide ion overlaps with the π system of the ring.
The negative charge is spread into the ring. This stabilises the phenoxide ion.
Phenol is therefore more acidic than an alcohol, where the charge stays on oxygen.
Phenol is less acidic than a carboxylic acid, where the charge is spread over two oxygen atoms.
Phenol is a weak acid that reacts with NaOH but not with carbonates.
The phenoxide ion is stabilised by delocalisation into the ring.

sections.heading: Why phenol substitutes more easily than benzene

blocks.text: Phenol reacts with bromine and nitric acid under much milder conditions than benzene. The explanation is the lone pair on oxygen.

items: A lone pair in a p orbital on the oxygen overlaps with the delocalised π system of the ring.
This donates electron density into the ring, so the ring has a **higher electron density** than benzene.
The ring is more susceptible to attack by electrophiles, and it polarises Br₂ so it does not need a catalyst.

rows: Br₂ with a halogen carrier such as FeBr₃
Aqueous bromine at room temperature, no catalyst

items: Bromine water is decolourised and a **white precipitate** of 2,4,6-tribromophenol forms.
Nitration of phenol needs no concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst.
The –OH group directs the new groups to the 2-, 4- and 6-positions.
Oxygen's lone pair donates electron density into the ring.
Phenol reacts with bromine water and dilute nitric acid, with no catalyst.
Bromine water gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

blocks.text: A group already on the ring decides where the next group goes, and how fast it goes. Pick a substituent to see its effect.

diagram.alt: A predictor. Pick a substituent on a benzene ring to see whether it donates or withdraws electrons, how it changes reactivity and where a second group goes.
diagram.prompt: Pick a substituent on the benzene ring.

items: **Electron-donating** groups (–OH, –NH₂, alkyl) push electron density into the ring. They direct to the **2- and 4-positions**.
**Electron-withdrawing** groups (–NO₂, –COOH, –COR) pull electron density from the ring. They direct to the **3-position**.
With –OH and –NH₂, all of the 2-, 4- and 6-positions are activated, so three substituents can add.

items.text: Find the group on the ring, and decide whether it donates or withdraws electrons.
Donating groups send the new group to the 2- and 4-positions. Withdrawing groups send it to the 3-position.
In a synthesis, add the groups in the order that puts them in the right places.

items: Nitrobenzene is brominated at the 3-position, giving 3-bromonitrobenzene.
Methylbenzene is nitrated at the 2- and 4-positions.
To make 3-nitrobenzoic acid, oxidise methylbenzene to benzoic acid first, then nitrate. The –COOH group sends the –NO₂ group to the 3-position.
If methylbenzene is nitrated first and then oxidised, the nitro group ends up in the 2- or 4-position.
Electron-donating groups direct to 2- and 4-, and make the ring more reactive.
Electron-withdrawing groups direct to 3-, and make the ring less reactive.
The order of steps in a synthesis decides the position.

checks.q: Describe a test that distinguishes phenol from ethanoic acid, and give the result for each.
checks.a: Add sodium carbonate (or sodium hydrogencarbonate). Ethanoic acid fizzes, giving off carbon dioxide. Phenol gives no reaction, because it is too weak an acid.

checks.q: Explain why phenol reacts with bromine water without a catalyst, but benzene does not.
checks.a: A lone pair on oxygen overlaps with the π system of the ring and donates electron density into it. The ring has a higher electron density than benzene, so it polarises Br₂ and is more readily attacked by the electrophile.

checks.q: Name the main organic product when nitrobenzene is brominated using bromine and iron(III) bromide, and explain the position of the bromine.
checks.a: 3-bromonitrobenzene. The –NO₂ group withdraws electron density from the ring, so it directs the incoming electrophile to the 3-position.

blocks.text: This part covers the limits of what is expected for directing effects.

items: Know the 2- and 4-directing effect of –OH and –NH₂, and the 3-directing effect of –NO₂.
You are not expected to know other electron-donating or electron-withdrawing groups. Data is supplied in the examination.
Explain the greater ease of phenol in terms of the ring being more susceptible to attack, with electron-pair donation from an oxygen p orbital to the π system.
Nitration of phenol needs dilute nitric acid only, and gives 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol.

blocks.text: This part covers the bromine water reaction in the form it is examined.

items: Phenol and bromine water react at room temperature to give 2,4,6-tribromophenol and HBr.
The observation is a white precipitate and the orange colour of bromine disappearing.
Compare benzene: it needs bromine with a catalyst, and gives only a monobromo product.

blocks.text: This part covers making phenol, more reactions of phenol, and relative acidities.

items.text: Phenylamine with HNO₂ (from NaNO₂ and dilute acid) below 10 °C gives a diazonium salt.
Warming the diazonium salt with water gives phenol.

blocks.text: Other phenolic compounds, such as naphthol, react in the same way. Apply the reactions of phenol to them.

items: Order of acidity: carboxylic acids > phenol > water > ethanol.
In ethoxide the alkyl group pushes electrons onto oxygen, so the charge is concentrated and the ion is unstable. Ethanol is the weakest acid.
In phenoxide the charge is partly spread into the ring, so phenol is more acidic than water and ethanol.
Phenol is too weak to react with carbonates. Its position is between the carboxylic acids and water.
